segments.summary: Freeman says records erased regional band styles and that Coltrane imitators made Trane himself more popular.

segments.chapter: Chicago repertoire, bands and the end of the big-band era
segments.title: Chicago local bands: King Fleming, Red Saunders, Jimmy Brinkley
segments.summary: He names the three local bands that mattered and says he played in King Fleming's.

segments.chapter: Chicago repertoire, bands and the end of the big-band era
segments.title: King Kolax recruits Gene Ammons; Freeman stays in school
segments.summary: Kolax came to DuSable for the two tenor hotshots; Jug left, and Freeman stayed to finish school.

segments.chapter: Chicago repertoire, bands and the end of the big-band era
segments.title: Paying Dyett for the stolen clarinet with arrangements
segments.summary: Freeman paid off the stolen clarinet by writing about twelve arrangements for Dyett's band.

segments.chapter: Chicago repertoire, bands and the end of the big-band era
segments.title: Gene Ammons, Billy Eckstine's band and the Chicago nucleus of Dizzy's band
segments.summary: They discuss Jug's path from Kolax to Eckstine and Red Top, and how Diz drew on Hines, Eckstine and Kolax alumni.

segments.chapter: Bird, Ben Webster and the 1950s decline
segments.title: Bird's praise and Freeman's first night playing with Bird
segments.summary: He confirms the quote that Bird liked his playing and tells how every horn player crowded the stand when he played with Bird.

segments.chapter: Bird, Ben Webster and the 1950s decline
segments.title: Bird and Ben Webster filling the Pershing without a microphone
segments.summary: Freeman marvels at their volume and recalls drinking with Ben Webster at the Pershing.

segments.chapter: Bird, Ben Webster and the 1950s decline
segments.title: Ben Webster says both he and Bird studied with Lester Young's father
segments.summary: Webster tells Freeman, with a caveat, about his link to Pres and Bird through Lester's father.

segments.chapter: Bird, Ben Webster and the 1950s decline
segments.title: Embouchure, double lip and Link mouthpieces
segments.summary: They discuss double-lip playing and Dyett's reaction, metal mouthpieces and Freeman's fifty-year-old Link.

segments.chapter: Bird, Ben Webster and the 1950s decline
segments.title: Young Chicago altoists in Bird's mode who died young
segments.summary: They try to recall a Bird-like altoist, with talk of Nicky Hill and drug casualties of the period.

segments.chapter: Bird, Ben Webster and the 1950s decline
segments.title: Sonny Rollins and Booker Little in Chicago
segments.summary: Coleman cites Rollins's book about practicing in Chicago; Freeman recalls Booker Little at McKee's D. J. Lounge.

segments.chapter: Bird, Ben Webster and the 1950s decline
segments.title: The Cottage Grove clubs fade after Bird's death; Clifford Brown's visit
segments.summary: Freeman says Bird's death took the enthusiasm from the music, and recalls Clifford Brown visiting the Pershing before his fatal crash.

segments.chapter: Bird, Ben Webster and the 1950s decline
segments.title: Navarro, McGhee and Diz; why the music declined
segments.summary: Freeman says the bebop figures faded in the early 1950s and singers and rock and roll came in.

segments.chapter: Bird, Ben Webster and the 1950s decline
segments.title: Miles Davis from the cool to the electric band
segments.summary: He recalls progressive jazz, then a Miles gig where he emceed, with Cicely Tyson in the wings, and the electric music.

segments.chapter: Chicago pianists, Tatum and talent versus practice
segments.title: Jack DeJohnette and Herbie Hancock from Chicago
segments.summary: Freeman says Jack played piano with him, and Herbie came from Evanston, not the clubs.

segments.chapter: Chicago pianists, Tatum and talent versus practice
segments.title: Miles's saxophonists after Coltrane; Sam Rivers
segments.summary: They discuss Shorter, Coleman, Rivers and Tony Williams's role in getting Rivers hired.

segments.chapter: Chicago pianists, Tatum and talent versus practice
segments.title: Sam Rivers and his wife Bea
segments.summary: Both praise Sam Rivers's far-out music, and Freeman recalls staying with him in New York and his years on the scene.

segments.chapter: Chicago pianists, Tatum and talent versus practice
segments.title: Playing piano first; Prentice McCarey on 55th Street
segments.summary: Freeman talks of his piano facility, marriage reception at a 55th Street club and pianist Prentice McCarey.

segments.chapter: Chicago pianists, Tatum and talent versus practice
segments.title: The night Art Tatum played all night at his club
segments.summary: McCarey brings Tatum, who plays until daybreak on a damaged piano; Freeman calls it unreal.

segments.chapter: Chicago pianists, Tatum and talent versus practice
segments.title: Tatum's gift and practice; Horowitz
segments.summary: They discuss Tatum's technique, Horowitz's admiration and Tatum's remark that he got it by practice.

segments.chapter: Chicago pianists, Tatum and talent versus practice
segments.title: Parker said it was practice
segments.summary: Coleman tells of Bird's interview with Paul Desmond saying he practiced 14-18 hours a day.

segments.chapter: Chicago pianists, Tatum and talent versus practice
segments.title: Child prodigies, gift and reincarnation
segments.summary: From his 1980s school clinics, Freeman discusses young kids who play, and his belief in transmigrated souls.

segments.chapter: Chicago pianists, Tatum and talent versus practice
segments.title: The power of music: marches, movies, Richard Pryor
segments.summary: They talk about march music's effect on soldiers, film scores and a Pryor joke.

segments.chapter: Open sets, touring and Sweet Basil
segments.title: The 'horses' and why Freeman won't play at his own sets
segments.summary: Freeman explains that he lets others play and keeps his horn down after losing his mode.

segments.chapter: Open sets, touring and Sweet Basil
segments.title: Visitors who wait all week to play: Billy Foulkes and Henry Pride
segments.summary: Out-of-town players come to play a prepared tune, sometimes not knowing it.

segments.chapter: Open sets, touring and Sweet Basil
segments.title: John Young's Invitation in the wrong key and ending a set
segments.summary: Freeman cuts a set short and pretends to be drunk to rescue a player, and describes managing open sets.

segments.chapter: Open sets, touring and Sweet Basil
segments.title: How his open sets began and why he calls them parties
segments.summary: He says open sets are old tradition and he now lets the 'horses' take over.

segments.chapter: Open sets, touring and Sweet Basil
segments.title: Joe Segal and the Jazz Showcase
segments.summary: Segal dislikes the jam portion but has softened; talk of Joe Lovano.

segments.chapter: Open sets, touring and Sweet Basil
segments.title: Milt Trenier's band and Richard Pryor on the bill
segments.summary: Freeman played with Milt Trenier from 1965 to 1969, with Pryor as an act on the bills.

segments.chapter: Open sets, touring and Sweet Basil
segments.title: Road work: Chico Freeman, abroad and one-off hires
segments.summary: Freeman says he mostly toured alone, hired by agencies, and with Chico at Ronnie Scott's.

segments.chapter: Open sets, touring and Sweet Basil
segments.title: Playing 60/40 and audience demands that he play
segments.summary: Freeman explains why he refuses to always play what others want and how his jam sessions caused problems.

segments.chapter: Open sets, touring and Sweet Basil
segments.title: Sweet Basil and Melissa Slocum
segments.summary: He defies the owners at Sweet Basil, where players jam, including bassist Melissa Slocum.

segments.chapter: Harmony lessons, development and recordings
segments.title: Learning to second a melody from Frederico
segments.summary: Asked when he could first get through tunes, he describes Frederico teaching him harmony by form and by ear.

segments.chapter: Harmony lessons, development and recordings
segments.title: Continuity of idea and Frederico's back-room lessons
segments.summary: Coleman names continuity of idea; Freeman recalls months of lessons in the dressing room while Frederico partied.

segments.chapter: Harmony lessons, development and recordings
segments.title: Big bands under King Fleming and Jimmy Brinkley; creating the fourth saxophone part
segments.summary: Freeman learned section playing and harmony in big bands at 13 or 14.

segments.chapter: Harmony lessons, development and recordings
segments.title: Choral playing and hymn harmony with Dyett
segments.summary: He praises Dyett's training in four-part hymns and spirituals as the best lesson in harmony.

segments.chapter: Harmony lessons, development and recordings
segments.title: Chris Anderson and Chicago pianists who worked with Freeman
segments.summary: He names blind pianist Chris Anderson, Ahmad Jamal, Andrew Hill and others he learned from.

segments.chapter: Harmony lessons, development and recordings
segments.title: Playing tunes his own way, like Bird
segments.summary: He says Bird played his tunes differently each time and he learned them by ear.

segments.chapter: Harmony lessons, development and recordings
segments.title: John Young taping Freeman and his late development
segments.summary: Young records every night from 1972, and listening back changed Freeman's playing.

segments.chapter: Harmony lessons, development and recordings
segments.title: Refusing a tenor battle with Sonny Stitt at Ratso's
segments.summary: He declined Joe Segal's billing and introduced Stitt as the star.

segments.chapter: Harmony lessons, development and recordings
segments.title: Doin' It Right Now, the Rahsaan-produced album
segments.summary: They discuss the 1972 album and the Atlantic A&R man's pressure.

segments.chapter: Harmony lessons, development and recordings
segments.title: The 3-D alley cover and unsold albums
segments.summary: Freeman's tuxedo is rejected for a funky cover photo, and the album sells little.

segments.chapter: Philosophy, tone and closing
segments.title: Learning you cannot change things; fear of reaching the end of the quest
segments.summary: He says he is coming to accept he cannot change others, and worries expanding his playing approaches noise.

segments.chapter: Philosophy, tone and closing
segments.title: Passing on knowledge and not keeping jazz secret
segments.summary: His present goal is to help young players, he says, and jazz knowledge has been kept secret.

segments.chapter: Philosophy, tone and closing
segments.title: Good and bad, going commercial and no leveling off
segments.summary: He says you go up or down, and musicians who sell out rarely return.

segments.chapter: Philosophy, tone and closing
segments.title: How he developed his tone
segments.summary: Coleman asks about tone as energy; Freeman says it is a quest for a glorious sound.

segments.chapter: Philosophy, tone and closing
segments.title: Heaven on earth, jazz as a force for good
segments.summary: He says there will be jazz musicians in heaven on earth and doesn't like the word jazz.

segments.chapter: Philosophy, tone and closing
segments.title: Intuition, logic and the feminine side
segments.summary: He recounts an argument with a woman about logic and intuition.

segments.chapter: Philosophy, tone and closing
segments.title: His daughter's illness and his meditation
segments.summary: Caring for his sick daughter led him to realize his music lacked his feminine side and ballads.

segments.chapter: Philosophy, tone and closing
segments.title: Record companies' demands and Coleman's offer
segments.summary: Labels demanded short tunes and no bass solos; he first hesitated to record.

segments.chapter: Philosophy, tone and closing
segments.title: Defiance, yin and yang, and the period after 1972
segments.summary: He says his defiance affected his sound and relates other breakthroughs.

segments.chapter: Philosophy, tone and closing
segments.title: When playing stopped being joyful in the 1980s
segments.summary: Playing became a chore and he sought soft applause, true feeling.

segments.chapter: Philosophy, tone and closing
segments.title: Losses in the 1990s
segments.summary: His uncle, daughter and mother died, and he nearly stopped playing.

segments.chapter: Philosophy, tone and closing
segments.title: The Chicago Jazz Festival set for his 75th and the feedback
segments.summary: The mic hummed and his best number was cut from the broadcast.

segments.chapter: Philosophy, tone and closing
segments.title: Tone as one's life: Billie Holiday, Bird and his divorce
segments.summary: He says tone carries one's ordeals and soul.

segments.chapter: Philosophy, tone and closing
segments.title: Wrapping up and setting up to play
segments.summary: Chatter about time, microphones and a missing strap.

segments.chapter: Philosophy, tone and closing
segments.title: Playing Billie's Bounce together
segments.summary: Freeman and Coleman play the tune and a ballad, closing the tape.
